title: Monotonic Stack: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
oneLiner: The biggest rectangle under a bar chart. Keep a stack of bars with increasing heights; when a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar it pops has found its right edge.
keyTakeaway: For each bar, the widest rectangle of its full height runs from the first shorter bar on its left to the first shorter bar on its right. A stack of increasing heights finds both at once: when bar i is shorter than the top, the top's right edge is i and its left edge is the new top below it. Pop, measure, repeat; a final height-0 bar flushes the stack. O(n).
explanation:
heights[i] is the height of bar i in a histogram where every bar is 1 wide. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the bars. For [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the answer is 10: height 5 across the bars 5 and 6.

Every candidate rectangle is limited by its shortest bar. So for each bar, ask: what is the widest rectangle whose height is exactly this bar's height? It extends left and right until it meets a shorter bar. Its width is (first shorter on the right) - (first shorter on the left) - 1. Checking every bar by scanning outwards is O(n²).

Both "first shorter" questions are next-smaller-element questions, which a monotonic stack answers in one pass (Next Greater Element and Daily Temperatures, flipped). Keep a stack of indices whose heights increase from bottom to top. When bar i is shorter than the bar on top, that top bar can't extend past i: pop it, its height is h, its right limit is i, and its left limit is the index now on top of the stack (or -1 if the stack is empty, meaning it reaches the left edge). Its area is h · (i - left - 1). Keep popping while the top is taller, then push i.

Bars still on the stack at the end reach the right edge. The neat way to handle them is to pretend there is one extra bar of height 0 at index n: it is shorter than everything, so it pops the whole stack through the same code. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n) time, O(n) stack.

This is also the core of Maximal Rectangle in a 0/1 matrix: treat each row as the floor of a histogram of consecutive 1s above it, and run this on every row.

The visualization runs [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]; the stack shows indices and heights.

recognitionSignals: "Largest rectangle", "maximal area" or "widest span" limited by the minimum in the span.
For each element you need the nearest smaller (or larger) element on both sides.
gotchas: The width after popping uses the NEW top as the left limit, not the popped index: width = i - stack.Peek() - 1, or i when the stack is empty.
Forgetting to flush the stack at the end misses rectangles that reach the right edge; a sentinel height 0 at index n handles it.
Pushing heights instead of indices loses the positions needed for the width.
confusableWith: Trapping Rain Water also looks at bars and their neighbours, but measures water above short bars, bounded by the taller bars around them.
Daily Temperatures pops when a LARGER value arrives (next greater); here you pop when a smaller bar arrives (next smaller), on both sides at once.

complexity.note: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so about 2n stack operations despite the nested loop. The stack can hold all n indices when the heights only increase.

referenceSolutions.python:
def largest_rectangle_area(heights):
    stack = []  # indices; their heights increase from bottom to top
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(heights) + 1):
        h = 0 if i == len(heights) else heights[i]  # a height-0 bar at the end flushes the stack
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            top = stack.pop()
            # Bar top spans from just after the new top (its first shorter bar on the left) to i - 1.
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            best = max(best, heights[top] * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return best
